Pherusa’s knife glides through the strawberries, effortlessly slicing them to the perfect size for a fruit salad. Behind her, the whisk knocks against the bowl as Mydei mixes the honeycake batter. They don’t normally talk beyond what’s necessary while in the kitchen together, both preferring to focus on cooking. It’s nice, she thinks, having helpful company that doesn’t chat her ear off every single time.

It’s even more nice when it’s the crown prince himself. She truly considers herself lucky, and she’s especially proud of how far he’s come. To think he used to try cracking eggs in the batter instead of using a flat surface. The memory of his first attempt makes her chuckle to this day.

He seems distracted this morning, though.

When checking the batter for eggshells, he stared a bit too deeply. While they discussed which fruits to put in the salad, he said blueberries twice. Even now, the whisk either moves too slow or too fast, the speed changing at odd intervals.

He’s not mulling over how to subtly mess up Phainon’s food again, is he? If he’s thinking this hard, he must be either running out of ideas or getting rusty. That’s not the Prince Mydeimos she knows. He should be quicker on his feet than this.

Sure, she’ll usually salvage one of the sides on Phainon’s plate, but she does look forward to Mydei’s creativity in the kitchen. It’s not fun if he starts losing his touch.

Pherusa glances at him over her shoulder, eyes narrowed. He’s tense. “Mydeimos,” she calls, noting the barest hint of a flinch from him. “I know something’s on your mind.”

He pauses, then sighs. “It’s fine,” he mumbles, stirring with newfound vigour. “I’ve got it under control.”

That may technically be true, but she can still read him any day of the week.

“Care to share your latest endeavours?” She leans her hip against the counter. When he hesitates, she prods, “Is it about your Deliverer?”

“My—?” He splutters, whirling around to face her. Flushed cheeks, furrowed eyebrows, refusal to meet her eyes… She got him. Mydei groans.

Pherusa, on the other hand, is the picture of smugness. She throws her head back and laughs. “Come now, Mydeimos. It’s about time you gave him an answer, isn’t it? It’s been long enough.”

Six months, to be exact. Courtship tends to take longer for royalty, but considering the lack of parents and kingdom involved, many steps can be easily skipped. No extensive talks about royal duties, no lands or people to be assimilated if Phainon were also royalty, no travelling long distances for either of them. They don’t need approval from the officials in court or anyone else for that matter, considering they’re both Chrysos Heirs, which is a first in Kremnoan history. It’s difficult to question the worthiness of an almost-demigod, especially one as universally trusted as Phainon.

It’s just the two of them.

Well, the two of them and the countless Kremnoans coaching Phainon in secret. Pherusa is one of them: she told him about weaving a wreath of myrtles to place around Mydei’s neck, both blessing their relationship and

calling forth endless victories in the battles ahead. It’s a step that typically takes place later in the process, and often a sign of impending proposal.

She sent that DM three weeks ago and got an enthusiastic “Thank you!!!” with five smiley faces in response. Has Phainon gone through with it already?

“I will.” Mydei’s face twists into a grimace. “That’s… what I’ve been thinking about, truth be told.”

Pherusa’s eyebrows nearly leap off her face. She didn’t expect to be this right. “Oh?”

He half turns away to absentmindedly scrape the sides of the bowl, something between longing and nervousness in his eyes. “I’d like to place an order for dinner three nights from now.” He purses his lips like it’s a pain to say the words aloud. “I would make it myself, but that’s when we return from a mission. I won’t have the energy.”

“You certainly won’t.” Pherusa crosses her arms. “I won’t have you dragging your injured self through my kitchen anyhow. So, what would you like?”

Mydei reaches for his pocket, freezes, moves his hand away, thinks better of it, then keeps going. He pulls out a big sticky note and wordlessly hands it to her. Not bothering to check her reaction, or perhaps too embarrassed to risk a glance, he shuffles to where they keep the pans.

Based on that odd spectacle, she can’t say she’s surprised by what’s written on the paper.

Before Phainon practically confessed his love in public, Mydei rarely placed orders at all. He either cooked on his own, to eat by himself in his chambers, or with her to eat with the other Chrysos Heirs. When he returned from missions, he’d just sleep off whatever injuries he had and wake up good as new before continuing on with his day, depending on the hour.

Now, he makes sure Phainon’s favourite foods are brought to Mydei’s chambers once a week along with Mydei’s typical dinner. He still helps her make it all, when he can. She repays him by helping him transport the food.

This time, it’s different.

The sticky note lists an entire pitcher of Mydei’s specific pomegranate juice, three of Phainon’s favourite dishes, and the name of a special layer cake traditionally served in the shape of a square: the portokalopita.

While oranges aren’t hard to come by in Okhema, they were difficult to acquire in Kremnos. So difficult, in fact, that the third Kremnoan king made it a routine to move Castrum Kremnos to the orchards of Kédros where they grew in abundance once a year. He even struck a deal with them, offering the finest Kremnoan weaponry and armour in exchange for ten percent of the harvest. Not just because oranges were a rare delicacy, but because his queen mentioned enjoying the juice in passing and wondered how it would taste as a syrup.

It didn’t take long for the portokalopita to be born. Within five harvests, the most skilled bakers in the royal kitchens created the queen’s favourite pastry. Over the centuries, children of Gorgo have used it to subtly accept romantic advances. If not a final answer, then at least an invitation to continue, depending on how early it was served to the suitor.

Pherusa looks up, watching Mydei gingerly place the pan on the stove and stare at it. When he reaches for the ladle and slowly closes his fingers around it, his eyes still boring holes into the pan, she snorts before she can stop herself. He instantly whips his head around with the weakest glare she’s ever seen.

“I’m not laughing at you,” Pherusa says, conspicuously hiding her face with the paper. Her shoulders shake and her lips tremble. “I… promise.”

Mydei groans and turns back around, scooping honeycake batter. “Just let it out and be done with it.”

He doesn’t need to ask her twice. She releases the guffaws stuck in her mouth, still hiding her face just in case, and takes a couple of deep breaths. After clearing her throat, she says, “My apologies. Your order isn’t a problem at all, Mydeimos. I would be honoured to complete it for you.” She grins, lowering the paper. “But you don’t have to be so shy about it! I figured this time would come sooner or later.”

Four honeycakes land in the pan, but she doesn’t hear them sizzle. He doesn’t seem to notice. “Oh, really? Have you been watching us like everyone else seems to be?”

Pherusa flicks a dismissive hand. “I hardly need to. It’s been so long, yet I haven’t heard a word of complaint about him from you. You’re not one to string poor affectionate souls along, are you?”

Mydei huffs. “Of course not.”

“I rest my case.” Pherusa shrugs and returns to her fruit, carefully folding the note into her pocket. “By the way, you might want to check the stove.”

“The stove?” Mydei looks around himself with hovering hands, muttering, “What’s wrong with the stove…?”

Pherusa presses her lips firmly together, cutting strawberries with a wobbly smile. She hears the sharp beep of the stove, frenzied scraping, and an exasperated curse. It’s a miracle that she refrains from laughing at all.

No matter how old he gets or what his hectic life throws at him, he’s still the same boy who struggles to voice his own deep feelings.

The aromatic orange syrup spills over the sides of the ladle as Pherusa steadily lifts it out of the bowl. She waits for it to collect at the bottom, dripping back down until the stream slows to a stop, then holds it over the portokalopita for a controlled pour.

This is always the most satisfying part. She wishes she could make soaked cakes every night.

The cold syrup fully sinks into the steaming hot cake, a nice and flavourful splotch, before she goes back for another dip. Another pour. Another dip. Another pour.

All the other dishes are ready and laid out on the wide tray with a pitcher of Mydei’s pomegranate juice in the corner. After the cake, the only thing left is to write the note to be served along with it.

She didn’t notice it when he first gave her the sticky note, but later that day, she had the mind to flip the paper over and read the other side. The light of Kephale’s Dawn Device had shone just right, making the words on the back appear in a faded mirror. There, she found a message he requested to have her write in Kremnoan. It wasn’t perfect, but she didn’t mind cleaning it up. She knows what it’s meant to say.

Once the soaking phase is complete, she places the cake in the icebox for chilling. It doesn’t need to be borderline frozen, just cold enough for the syrup to thicken while she finds a pen and paper. Her journey leads her out of the kitchens.

As she walks, she can’t help the pride swelling in her chest. She has seen him grow from a tactless yet earnest child into such a well-rounded man that she can hardly believe his progress. He’s made friends, lost them, tried again, and ended up meeting his match.

His true match.

She hardly needs to speak for the combat side. Their duel when they first met is still brought up around the average Kremnoan dinner table to this day. It’s spoken of with wonder, awe, and the utmost respect. More than a few people in the older crowd have nostalgically compared it to the late King Eurypon and Queen Gorgo in their early days.

From what she’s seen of them, their personalities complement each other perfectly. They’re similar where it matters most and are different enough to

have an interesting dynamic. They exist in such clear harmony that anyone would have a hard time believing they didn’t get together sooner.

And now, this is the moment the Kremnoan detachment has been waiting for. Not just because their courtship has set the world wound web on fire, but because it’s Mydeimos. He’s their leader, their king, the man they trust with all their lives, with their beloved nation, with a thousand years of history.

Aside from returning to Kremnos, all so many of them have wished for is to see him happy. After everything he’s done for his people, especially since their arrival at Okhema, it’s the absolute least he deserves.

Pherusa is certain that his mother, bless her heroic soul, must be smiling in the afterlife.

She stops at a side table at the end of the hallway and tugs on the drawer. Exactly where she thought they’d be.

Taking up a pen, she twirls it in her fingers before writing the message:

May the blade forged of our love, tempered by the hardships we overcome, defeat all who stand in our way.

My blind spots are yours to protect.
